en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Time, 3. The Question on Knowledge and Wisdom (Ñāṇapaññāpañha) "Venerable sir, what is knowledge (ñāṇa) and what is wisdom (paññā)? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the meaning of what has been heard; wisdom is the penetration of the meaning of what has been understood. "But, venerable sir, is there a difference between knowledge and wisdom, or are they one and the same? "There is a difference, great king, between knowledge and wisdom; they are not one and the same. "How so, venerable sir? Please give me an illustration. "It is as if, great king, a man were to enter a forest of sal trees. There he would see the flowers of a sal tree, but not its fruit. He would think: ‘These are the flowers of this sal tree, but where is its fruit? Then, after some time, he would see the fruit. He would think: ‘This is the fruit of that sal tree. Now, great king, is there a difference between the flower and the fruit, or are they one and the same? "There is a difference, venerable sir, between the flower and the fruit; they are not one and the same. "In the same way, great king, knowledge is the understanding of the meaning of what has been heard; wisdom is the penetration of the meaning of what has been understood. Thus, great king, there is a difference between knowledge and wisdom; they are not one and the same. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the Four Noble Truths; wisdom is the penetration of those Four Noble Truths. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka); wisdom is the penetration of the Three Baskets. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana); wisdom is the penetration of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda); wisdom is the penetration of dependent origination. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the causes of suffering; wisdom is the penetration of the cessation of suffering. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the path; wisdom is the penetration of the path. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the fruits of the spiritual life (sāmaññaphala); wisdom is the penetration of the fruits of the spiritual life. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the Dhamma; wisdom is the penetration of the Dhamma. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the Teacher's instructions; wisdom is the penetration of the Teacher's instructions. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures; wisdom is the penetration of the meaning of the scriptures. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the words; wisdom is the penetration of the words. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the letters; wisdom is the penetration of the letters. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the conventional truth (sammutisacca); wisdom is the penetration of the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca). "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammanvaya-ñāṇa);

wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of phenomena. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of meanings (atthānvaya-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of meanings. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttianvaya-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of language. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānanvaya-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of self-confidence (vebhabyānvaya-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of self-confidence. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the meaning (atthavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the meaning. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttivebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of language. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammanvayavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the meaning (atthānvayavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the meaning. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttianvayavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of language. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānanvayavebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhammavebhabyāvebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of the meaning (atthavebhabyāvebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of the meaning. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttivebhabyāvebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of language. "Venerable sir, what is knowledge and what is wisdom? "Knowledge, great king, is the understanding of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānavebhabyāvebhabyā-ñāṇa); wisdom is the penetration of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, has wisdom also arisen?
"Yes, Great King, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, wisdom has also arisen."
“Venerable sir, is that which is knowledge the same as wisdom?
“Yes, great king, that which is knowledge is the same as wisdom.
“But venerable sir, for one in whom that very knowledge and that very wisdom have arisen, would he be deluded, or would he not be deluded?”
“In some cases, great king, one might be confused; in other cases, one would not be confused.
“Where, venerable sir, would one be confused?

“In regard to crafts or fields of knowledge previously unknown, great king, or in regard to a direction never before traveled, or in regard to a name or designation never before heard, one would be confused.”
“Where would one not be deluded?
“In that which has been accomplished by that wisdom, O Great King—whether it be as ‘impermanent,’ or ‘suffering,’ or ‘non-self’—there one would not be deluded.
“But where, venerable sir, does his delusion go?”
“Delusion, great king, ceases right there as soon as knowledge has arisen.
“Give me an illustration,” [the king said].
“Just as if, great king, some man were to bring a lamp into a house that was in darkness; then the darkness would cease and light would appear.”
“In the same way, Great King, as soon as knowledge has arisen, delusion ceases right there.
“But where does wisdom go, venerable sir?

“Wisdom too, Great King, having performed its own function, ceases right there; however, that which was accomplished by that wisdom—whether it be ‘impermanence,’ ‘suffering,’ or ‘non-self’—that does not cease.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you said— that wisdom, having performed its function, ceases right there,
but that which was accomplished by that wisdom— namely, ‘it is impermanent,’ ‘it is suffering,’ or ‘it is non-self’— does not cease,
please provide an illustration for this.”
“Just as, Great King, if some man wishing to send a letter at night were to summon a scribe,
light a lamp, and have the letter written; and once the letter was written, he were to extinguish the lamp— even though the lamp is extinguished,
the letter would not be destroyed.”

“In the same way, great king, wisdom, having performed its own function, ceases right there; but that which was accomplished by that wisdom—namely, ‘it is impermanent,’ or ‘it is suffering,’ or ‘it is non-self’—that does not cease.
“Give me another simile.
“It is as if, great king, in the eastern provinces, people were to place five water-pots in each house...”
They set aside the materials for plastering in order to extinguish the fire; when the house is ablaze, they throw those five water-jars over the house, and then the fire is extinguished.
Now, Great King, would it occur to those people, "We shall perform the function of a jar with those jars again"?"
“Certainly not, venerable sir; those jars are of no use to you—what need have you for those jars?

“Great king, just as there were five water jars, so should the five faculties be regarded: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Just as those men were, so should the practitioner of yoga be regarded.”
"Just as fire is to be regarded [in this way], so too are the defilements.
Just as fire is extinguished by five pots of water, so too are the defilements extinguished by the five faculties; and once extinguished, the defilements do not arise again.

Even so, Great King, wisdom, having performed its own function, ceases right there; but that which was accomplished by that wisdom—whether it be 'impermanence,' 'suffering,' or 'non-self'—does not cease."
“Give me another simile. “Just as if, great king,
a physician were to take five kinds of root medicines, approach a sick man, grind those five root medicines,
and give them to the sick man to drink, and by means of them he would expel the humors— what do you think?”
“Great King, would it not occur to that physician: ‘I shall again perform the work of medicine with those five root-medicines’?
“No indeed, Bhante; those five root-medicines are sufficient; what need is there for those five root-medicines?

“Great King, just as the five root-medicines are, so should the five faculties be regarded: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Just as the physician is, so should the practitioner of yoga be regarded.”
Just as with the disease, so should the defilements be regarded.
Just as the man who is ill, so should the worldling be regarded.

Just as the humors of the sick man are expelled by the five root medicines, and once the humors have been expelled the sick man becomes healthy, so too are the defilements expelled by the five faculties; and once the defilements have been expelled, they do not arise again.

“In the same way, great king, wisdom, having performed its own function, ceases right there; but that which was accomplished by that wisdom—namely, ‘it is impermanent,’ or ‘it is suffering,’ or ‘it is non-self’—that does not cease.
“Give me a further simile,” [the king said].
“Suppose, great king, a warrior engaged in battle were to enter the fray taking five arrows with him to strike down the enemy host.”
To conquer [the enemy], suppose that warrior, having entered the battle, were to shoot those five arrows and by them the opposing army were broken;
what then, Great King, would this soldier engaged in battle think: ‘I shall again perform the work of an arrow with those arrows’?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; those arrows are of no use, what need have you for those arrows?

“Great king, just as there are five arrows, so too should the five faculties be regarded: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Great king, just as a warrior engaged in battle, so should the practitioner of yoga be regarded.”
"Just as the enemy army is to be regarded, so too are the defilements to be seen.
Just as the enemy army is broken by means of five arrows, so too are the defilements broken by means of the five faculties; and once the defilements are broken, they do not arise again.

In the same way, Great King, wisdom, having performed its own function, ceases right there; but that which has been accomplished by that wisdom—whether it be 'impermanence,' 'suffering,' or 'non-self'—does not cease."
“Beautiful, venerable Nāgasena!
Thus ends the third question on knowledge and wisdom.
